To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
bilinguals show a neural adaptation to language demands that is specific to language use contexts and is reflected by a neural reserve in language control.
the neural control of language is implemented by a network of regions that is sensitive to the language demands of the task and the context of use.
the neural control of language in bilinguals is a complex process that involves a distributed set of regions that can be modulated depending on the demands of the interaction.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the neurocognitive mechanisms that support the control of language in bilinguals and the adaptive control hypothesis that predicts that the language control network is shaped by the demands of language use.
the neural mechanisms of language control and the adaptive control hypothesis that underlie the neurocognitive basis of bilingualism.
how language control is implemented in the brain and how it is affected by bilingualism.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the brain of bilinguals is not different from that of monolinguals but is more flexible and adaptable.
the neural reserve hypothesis is supported by evidence of adaptive changes in the language control network.
the neural control system of bilingualism is a highly adaptive system that can be modulated to meet the demands of different language control situations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
bilinguals are able to flexibly adapt to the control demands in different interactional contexts.
the brain adapts to the demands of the bilingual experience by developing a language control network that can flexibly and efficiently manage the control of two languages.
the language control network, as a whole, is a neural marker of bilingualism, and its adaptive plasticity is a marker of bilingual cognitive reserve.
The main takeaway from our work is that
language control in bilingualism is not only an interesting phenomenon to investigate but also an ideal paradigm to understand the brain's ability to adapt to new situations.
the language control network is a dynamic and adaptive system that changes with the demands of the task and the interactional context.
the brain of the bilinguals is not only more plastic than previously thought but also more efficient in the control of multiple languages.
